claims.claim: The ICO updated its international transfers guidance on 15 January 2026, with a three-step test: UK GDPR applies, the sender initiates a transfer outside the UK, and the receiver is a separate legal person. A UK branch sending data to its overseas head office is not a restricted transfer.
claims.source: Commentary by Kennedys, Freshfields, McDermott Will & Emery and White & Case on the ICO guidance, seen through search results, November 2026. ico.org.uk was not reachable from the build environment.

claims.claim: Section 85 and Schedule 7 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 replaced Article 45 with Articles 45A and 45B and set the data protection test: protection 'not materially lower' than under UK GDPR. In force from 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82).
Transfers to an EEA state are treated as approved by regulations under Article 45A (DPA 2018 Schedule 21, paragraphs 4 and 5).
The European Commission renewed its adequacy decisions for the UK on 19 December 2025, until 27 December 2031.
claims.source: Hunton, Freeths, RPC and Computer Weekly reports, seen through search results, November 2026.

concept_html:
Talent data rarely stays in one country. A shared service centre runs payroll, a vendor hosts the learning platform, a group company abroad builds the dashboards. UK GDPR Chapter V controls these flows as restricted transfers.

Since the ICO's January 2026 guidance, a three-step test tells you whether a flow is restricted. Answer yes to all three and it is:

  1. Does UK GDPR apply to your processing of the data?
  2. Do you initiate the transfer, by sending the data or by making it available to someone outside the UK?
  3. Is the receiver a separate legal person, such as another company in your group?

A UK branch sending data to its own overseas head office fails step 3, so it is not restricted. A UK company sending data to a sister company in India is restricted, even inside one group.

A restricted transfer needs one of three routes:

  • Adequacy regulations: UK law approves the destination. Transfers to the EEA countries are treated as approved.
  • Appropriate safeguards: a contract such as the International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA), plus a check that protection is "not materially lower" than in the UK. Lesson E3-L2 covers how to choose.
  • Exceptions: narrow, for occasional transfers. Explicit consent rarely works for employees, for the reason lesson E1-L2 gives.

The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 set the "not materially lower" standard. It took effect on 5 February 2026.

The direction matters. The EU's adequacy decision for the UK, renewed to 27 December 2031, covers data flowing into the UK from the EU. It says nothing about data you send out.

title: Restricted transfers, when people data leaves the UK
why_html: A UK HR team gave a sister company in another country read access to a performance dashboard "so they could help". Nobody saw it as a transfer, because no file moved. An audit found 9,000 employee records available to a separate legal entity with no contract in place. Access was withdrawn for three months while legal put an agreement in place.
